reading.identification: Groot Vleeshuis, Ghent: a late-Gothic (1407-1419) brick and Tournai-bluestone civic butchers' hall, one great storey under a very tall steep slate roof, its Vleeshuistragel flank articulated by the 16 small stepped-gable penshuisjes of the 1540s, now in public market / regional-produce-centre use.
reading.notes:
SET B IS A DIFFERENT BUILDING - discarded. It shows a ~12 m wide, two-storey yellow machine-brick block with a slate mansard, pedimented dormer, segmental brick relieving arches and a "'t STAPELhuis" fascia sign. That is incompatible with a 58.5 m frontage, 72.1 x 12.9 m footprint, 16.0 m confirmed height, building=public hall. The street photo is mis-georeferenced; none of its wall material, window size, sill or ground-floor evidence has been used. Consequently every field except roof form is inferred from knowledge of the Groot Vleeshuis, and confidence is capped accordingly.

SEEN (set A only, massing scale): one long unbroken steeply-pitched slate roof plane whose ridge runs the length of the block, i.e. parallel to both Vleeshuistragel and the Groentenmarkt frontage; a repeating fine-grained file of small gabled units with dark window openings along the flank, roughly 3.5-4 m on centre; a continuous low plinth at ground level. The plate cannot resolve mullions, reveal depth, bond or stone dressing, and it crops the right-hand end of the range, so the bay count is a reconstruction, not a tally.

GRAMMAR NOTES:
- storeys=1 honours building:levels=1 and is physically right: one great hall volume, not stacked floors. 7.0 m eaves plus the roof accounts for the 16.0 m confirmed height. upper_height_m is unused at count=1 and is a placeholder in range.
- The 16 bays are the penshuisjes, each a narrow attached unit with its own stepped gablet standing proud of the hall's flank wall. These gablets are the most important geometry on this building - they are the silhouette and what a rotated camera sees, and they sit firmly in the >10 cm explicit-geometry regime. Do not flatten them into texture on a long box; that is the visible-primitive failure this facade is most exposed to. roof.form=gabled describes the main hall roof only; the gablet range must come from the bay rhythm.
- reveal_class=deep is structural, not a photo guess: medieval load-bearing brick with bluestone surrounds gives ~0.25 m returns. Those reveals plus sills and the string course at gablet springing are the wedges that will dominate off-specular scatter into Vleeshuistragel at 3.8 m standoff.
- trim=marble is the enum's closest dielectric stand-in for Tournai bluestone (dense carboniferous limestone) used for plinth, window surrounds, sills, string courses and gable copings. Not decorative marble.
- roughness_mm=6 covers hand-made brick with weathered recessed joints and the coursing of the stone dressings. This is the 1-10 cm regime and must stay a roughness/scattering coefficient - do not mesh the bond.
- ground_floor=institutional_portal reflects the monumental arched hall entrance on the Groentenmarkt front. The Vleeshuistragel flank at ground level is largely closed backs and small doors of the penshuisjes, so detail placed against the fronting path should read closer to blank-with-small-doors, reserving the portal for the market frontage.
- Clutter: fronting_street is a 3.8 m gravel path with car_access=none, inside Ghent's pedestrianised medieval core. Place no vehicles. Appropriate clutter is pedestrian - bicycles leaned and racked, bollards, waste bins, cafe seating and A-boards spilling from the Groentenmarkt side, wear on the gravel. The black VW in set B belongs to a different city block.
